title: Methods of Separation in Everyday Life
intro: Most things around us are mixtures — tea has milk, sugar, and water; salt comes packed with bits of dirt. This chapter explains why and how we separate one thing from another and shows the everyday tricks behind these methods.

sections.heading: Why We Separate Mixtures
bullets: Most natural and packaged substances are mixtures — milk, salt, tea, dal — not pure substances.
We separate to remove harmful parts (stones from rice), to keep only what we want (cream from milk), or to get a pure substance for science use.
The right method depends on what's in the mixture and what properties differ between its parts.
Two parts that differ in size, colour, density, or solubility can usually be separated.

sections.heading: Hand-picking and Sieving
bullets: Hand-picking works when one part is large and easy to spot — pulling out small stones from a bowl of dal.
It is slow but accurate for small amounts.
Sieving uses a mesh that lets small pieces pass through and stops bigger ones.
Flour mills use large sieves to separate fine flour from bran and lumps.
Sand and pebbles can be separated by sieving in the same way.

sections.heading: Threshing and Winnowing
bullets: Farmers separate grain from harvested plants by threshing — beating or crushing the stalks to release grain.
After threshing, grain still has light husk (chaff) mixed with it.
Winnowing uses wind: heavier grain falls straight down, while lighter chaff is blown a little farther.
On windless days, large machines blow air to do the same job.
These methods rely on the difference in weight between grain and chaff.

sections.heading: Sedimentation and Decantation
bullets: When you mix soil with water and let it stand, soil settles at the bottom — this is sedimentation.
Slowly pouring out the clear water on top, without disturbing the settled solid, is called decantation.
These two methods together are an easy way to separate insoluble solids from a liquid.
Loading a filter paper afterwards picks up any fine bits left behind.

sections.heading: Filtration
bullets: Filtration uses a porous material like filter paper or fine cloth.
The liquid passes through the holes, and the solid bits get caught.
Tea strainers, coffee filters, and water purifiers all use filtration.
It is the best method for fine, insoluble solids that won't settle quickly.
If the solid is dissolved (like sugar), filtration cannot separate it.

sections.heading: Evaporation and Crystallisation
bullets: Evaporation removes the liquid by letting it slowly turn into vapour, leaving the solid behind.
We make salt this way at the seacoast: seawater is collected in shallow pans, the Sun evaporates the water, and salt remains.
Crystallisation gives pure, neat solid pieces (crystals) when a saturated solution is allowed to cool slowly.
Salt and sugar from solution come out as small clear crystals.
Crystallisation is a neater, more useful version of plain evaporation when we want pure solid.

sections.heading: Combining Methods
bullets: Some mixtures need more than one method — separating sand and salt from water needs sedimentation, filtration, and evaporation in sequence.
First let the sand settle, decant the water, filter to remove fine particles, then evaporate the salty water to get salt.
Each step removes one part; the order matters.
Industries like sugar mills and water-treatment plants use long chains of separation steps.

key_takeaways: Most things we use are mixtures, and we separate them to remove harmful parts or get useful ones.
Hand-picking and sieving work for solid–solid mixtures with different sizes.
Threshing and winnowing use weight differences to separate grain from chaff.
Sedimentation, decantation, and filtration separate insoluble solids from liquids.
Evaporation and crystallisation recover dissolved solids like salt or sugar.
More complex mixtures need a sequence of methods — water, salt, and sand needs three steps.

glossary.definition: A combination of two or more substances that keep their own properties.
Removing unwanted bits from a mixture by hand, by sight.
Using a mesh to separate solids of different sizes.
Beating harvested plants to release grain from stalks and ears.
Using wind to separate heavier grain from lighter chaff.
The settling of insoluble solids at the bottom of a liquid when left undisturbed.
Pouring off the clear top liquid after sedimentation, without disturbing the solid.
Passing a mixture through a porous material to trap solids and let liquid pass.
Removing liquid from a mixture by letting it slowly turn into vapour.
Forming neat, pure solid crystals from a hot solution that is cooled slowly.
A liquid with a substance fully dissolved in it, like sugar in water.
